column4: The section’s named root ض ل ل (ḍ-l-l) appears in ضَلَلْنَا فِي الْأَرْضِ: the speakers treat being lost in earth as an end, while the verse makes that disappearance the question of renewed creation.

The section’s dictionary sense of ض ل ل includes the dead buried and hidden; this verse says what the earth diminishes of people remains in a preserving record, so hidden from sight does not mean lost to God.

The section pairs its named root ض ل ل with forgetting; Musa answers Firʿawn’s question about past generations in 20:51 by saying his Lord neither يَضِلُّ nor يَنسَى, so the vanished past is not lost to divine knowledge.

The section’s named root ص ر ط presents a road along which a traveler passes from sight; here people rush along الصراط after their eyes are obscured, separating movement on a way from the ability to see it.
The section says fabricated partners disappear from their worshippers at the gathering; this verse states وَضَلَّ عَنْهُم مَا كَانُوا يَفْتَرُونَ, making the vanished claim itself the focus.

The section describes Yusuf’s concealment in a well as a disappearance that leads to a destination; this verse shows the caravan’s water drawer finding him, so being out of sight has carried him into another people’s hands.

After Yusuf is put in the well, this verse says God reveals that he will later tell his brothers what they did while they remain unaware; the hidden traveler already has a destination beyond the brothers’ sight.
The section names غَيَابَتِ الْجُبِّ, the well’s hidden recess: the brothers propose putting Yusuf there so a caravan may take him, a concrete disappearance that is meant to lead somewhere.

The section distinguishes a traveler who vanishes from view while following a route from someone lost without knowing where he is going; this verse pictures a حَيْرَان person in the land while companions call him toward guidance.

The section’s named root ض ل ل has a dictionary branch for an event disappearing from memory; here أَنْ تَضِلَّ إِحْدَاهُمَا is paired with the other woman reminding her, showing how a lost recollection is recovered.

The section quotes the denial that people who disappear into earth can be recreated; this verse repeats the question about death and becoming dust, presenting burial as apparent disappearance before 50:4 answers it.
The section says the dead’s disappearance into earth is not the end but a way to meeting; this verse has people hurry out of their graves toward their Lord when the trumpet is blown.

After the emergence in 36:51, this verse identifies the graves as a seeming sleep and the awakening as the promise of the Most Merciful; its own contribution is naming the destination reached after concealment.

Following the blinded rush on the path in 36:66, this verse says that if God willed they could neither move forward nor return; it supplies a boundary between a traversable route and complete loss of movement.
The section’s road image distinguishes purposeful travel from losing one’s way; this verse contrasts someone moving face-down with someone walking upright on صِرَاطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ.
The section places the disappearance of false partners at the gathering; this verse stages that gathering and asks the associators where their claimed partners are.

This verse gives the associators’ denial in the gathering scene begun in 6:22; 6:24 then says their fabricated claims have vanished, so this row contributes the denial immediately before that exposure.
This verse names the Day of Recompense and the fire they enter; the following verse, 82:16, says they cannot be absent from it, fixing the referent of the section’s no-disappearance claim.
The section says no one can vanish from the Day of Recompense; this verse gives that boundary directly: وَمَا هُمْ عَنْهَا بِغَائِبِينَ.

The section’s dictionary examples include a thing lost in water and something gone from memory; this verse joins both in the fish forgotten by Moses and his companion as it takes its way into the sea.
The companion later says نسِيتُ الْحُوتَ and recounts that the fish took its way in the sea; his explanation makes the water-disappearance and lost memory in 18:61 explicit.
The section’s road traveler disappears from the observer yet has a destination; this verse describes each person striving toward his Lord and then meeting Him, giving travel an explicit endpoint.
The section presents the straight path as a route with an arrival; this verse joins the two details by saying God calls to the Abode of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path.

The section’s named root ص ر ط depicts a route that takes a traveler somewhere; here guidance leads from darkness to light and to the straight path, specifying the change and destination of the journey.
The section understands ص ر ط as a course that carries someone onward; this verse calls it the Lord’s straight path, with the following verse naming the abode of peace for those who reach it.
This verse names the Abode of Peace as the destination of the straight path in 6:126; its own contribution is showing where that directed travel arrives.
The section’s named root ص ر ط is used here for the straight path to which the Messenger calls people; the verse makes the route an offered direction rather than an aimless disappearance.
The section contrasts a path that reaches somewhere with being lost; this verse says those who reject the Hereafter turn aside from الصراط, naming the route’s contrary direction.
The section’s straight road carries a traveler toward an end; this verse commands that the wrongdoers be guided to صِرَاطِ الْجَحِيمِ, an explicitly contrary destination.

The section’s named root ض ل ل means being lost or out of sight, not simply the opposite of walking; this verse says God found the Prophet ضَالًّا and guided him, showing a lost state that can lead into guidance.
The section describes dalal as a person with no known destination; people here confess that their leaders أَضَلُّونَا السَّبِيلَا, identifying other people as the cause of their lost route.
The section’s named root ض ل ل is paired here with inability to find a way: the opponents have strayed and cannot find سَبِيلًا, matching loss as movement without a known destination.
The section’s named root ض ل ل is used with the way itself: whoever exchanges belief for disbelief has strayed from سَوَاءَ السَّبِيلِ, a direct instance of losing the route.

The section’s named root ض ل ل appears in the wish that others lose the way; this verse says some People of the Book want believers to تَضِلُّوا السَّبِيلَ, making misdirection an intended diversion from a route.
The section links ض ل ل to the traveler’s course; this verse describes people who strayed from the sound way and led many others astray, turning the path image into a chain of diverted travelers.
The section’s image is a path along which a traveler advances; Satan says he will sit in wait upon the straight path, placing an adversary directly on that route.
The section treats the path as a directed passage with an arrival; this verse describes revelation bringing people from darkness into light and to the path of the Mighty, Praiseworthy.

The section explains ص ر ط through the dictionary image of food swallowed and passing out of sight; Jonah is swallowed by the fish, a human disappearing inside a body while the following verses distinguish that from being lost forever.

After the fish swallows Jonah in 37:142, this verse says his being among the glorifiers is the condition that prevents permanent confinement; it supplies the route’s limit rather than leaving the disappearance final.
This verse completes the fish scene by setting the alternative duration, remaining in its belly until the day people are raised; the swallowed person’s disappearance has a boundary and release.

The section says a traveler can disappear from sight while still reaching a destination; Moses’ mother is told to cast him in the river with the promise إِنَّا رَادُّوهُ إِلَيْكِ, making the water journey purposeful.
This verse continues Moses’ river journey by showing Pharaoh’s household picking him up; it contributes the arrival after the child has been hidden from his mother’s sight.
This verse completes the river journey by returning Moses to his mother so her eyes may be comforted; the one lost from sight is shown to have reached the promised destination.

The section’s examples make disappearance different from erasure; the treasure hidden beneath the wall is preserved for two orphans until the right time, so concealment can protect what is meant to arrive.

The section contrasts a road that reaches its destination with loss that leaves no arrival; the disbelievers’ deeds are a mirage that seems to promise water, but when the seeker reaches it he finds nothing.

The section uses disappearance in water as an image of loss; after Pharaoh drowns, this verse says his body is saved as a sign for those who come later, a specific reversal of vanishing without trace.
The section describes what people falsely claim disappearing from them; this verse says they arrive alone, cannot see their claimed intercessors, and وَضَلَّ عَنْكُمْ مَا كُنْتُمْ تَزْعُمُونَ.

At the judgment gathering, this verse says people who had forgotten the meeting discover the truth and that their fabricated intercessors have vanished; it repeats the section’s disappearance of claims from their makers.
The section describes invented objects disappearing from their makers at judgment; this verse says وَضَلَّ عَنْهُم مَّا كَانُوا يَفْتَرُونَ when every soul faces what it did.
This verse says the wrongdoers lost themselves and their fabrications disappeared from them; it makes both kinds of loss in the section visible at once, the person and what the person invented.
The section describes false claims disappearing from their worshippers on the final day; this verse says their inventions are lost from them when they submit to God.
At the gathering, this verse says the proof is shown and what people invented has vanished from them; it gives the section’s lost claim a courtroom setting.
The section says false partners disappear from those who relied on them; when asked where they are, people here answer that they have departed from them and admit they had called on nothing.
This verse says what people invoked before has vanished from them and they have no escape; it directly parallels the section’s lost false objects and the boundary of judgment.
The section’s named root ض ل ل describes a traveler with no known way; at the gathering, God asks whether the worshipped beings led people astray or whether the people themselves ضَلُّوا السَّبِيلَ.

The worshipped beings answer the question in 25:17 by saying their followers forgot the reminder and became a people بُورًا; the response continues the scene of followers left without the destination they imagined.

The section distinguishes a way that reaches its end from a person led off course; here one who turns away from the reminder is paired with a satanic companion, setting up the diversion described in 43:37.
This verse says the companions turn people away from السَّبِيل while they think they are guided, a precise case of losing the route without knowing it.
The section’s named root ض ل ل pictures loss of direction; this verse negates that loss for the Prophet, so the route carrying revelation is distinguished from aimless wandering.
The section links losing the path with not knowing where one goes; this verse joins blindness in this life with greater ضَلَالًا عَنِ السَّبِيلِ in the next, extending the lost route beyond death.
The section’s named root ص ر ط appears in this chapter as the straight path of worship; this verse identifies the path whose visibility and traversal become the issue in 36:66.
When Abraham sees the star set, he fears being among الضَّالِّين unless his Lord guides him; the disappearing object becomes a concrete occasion for the section’s question of losing direction.
The section quotes the objection that people lost in earth cannot be recreated; this verse repeats the objection in terms of bones and fragments becoming a new creation.
In answer to the objection in 17:49, this verse says even stone or iron would not exceed God’s power to restore; it treats changed material as no escape from return.
This verse asks who will restore even a seemingly greater creation and answers, the One who created them the first time; it makes bodily change no barrier to return.
After the restoration exchange in 17:51, this verse says God will call people and they will respond with praise; it names the meeting that follows the apparent disappearance in death.
The section describes those who think burial is an end; this verse repeats their question whether they will be raised after dying and becoming dust and bones.
This verse gives the objectors’ conclusion that resurrection is an old fable; its own contribution is the denial that the section’s disappearance-under-earth image has a later destination.
The section’s buried dead are hidden from sight; this verse asks whether they will be raised after becoming dust and bones, repeating that disappearance as an objection.
This verse extends the objection in 37:16 to earlier generations, making the disappearance across generations part of the same question.
The answer to the dust-and-bones question is yes, and they will be humbled; this verse supplies the destination that the objectors deny.
This verse asks whether people will be raised after death and becoming dust and bones, directly matching the section’s scene of bodies disappearing into earth.
The question in 56:48 extends the dust objection to their forefathers, completing the scope of the denial in 56:47.
This verse answers by saying earlier and later generations will be gathered at an appointed day; the hidden dead have a specified gathering rather than an unknown end.
This verse names that gathering as the appointed meeting of the known Day; it completes the answer to the disappearance raised in 56:47–48.
The section says burial can look like disappearance without return; this verse voices the question whether people will be restored to their former state after death.
This verse sharpens the objection by asking about return after becoming decayed bones, matching the section’s burial image.
The objectors call resurrection كَرَّةٌ خَاسِرَةٌ, a losing return; this reverses the section’s distinction between aimless disappearance and a road that reaches its destination.
This verse presents the resurrection objection through decayed bones and a question about who can revive them, a direct counterpart to the section’s dead hidden in earth.
The answer says the one who created them the first time will revive them; the apparent loss of bodily form is not the end of their path.
This verse describes people as dead, then given life, then dying and being revived before returning to God; it makes earthly disappearance one stage in a movement to a destination.
This verse asks people to consider how God begins creation and repeats it; it treats apparent ending as a passage that can be followed by a new beginning.
This verse states that God begins creation and then repeats it; its own contribution is to make return after disappearance part of the same creative course.
The section treats earth as the place where bodies disappear; this verse says God gives life to earth after its death, reversing the image of ground as a final hiding place.
The section describes the dead as lost when buried; this verse reverses that concealment when the earth throws out its burdens.
After the earth casts out its burdens in 99:2, it reports its news in this verse; what was hidden under it becomes testimony.

After people see what they sent ahead, the disbeliever wishes he were dust; this reverses the section’s question of whether becoming dust is final, since the dust wish comes after judgment is visible.
The section makes disappearance and what remains perceptible; this verse gives a specific image of worldly growth becoming yellow and debris, then contrasts it with the enduring Hereafter.
The section asks what direction a journey finally takes; this verse says people prefer the nearer life, naming the pull toward an immediate destination.
This verse says the Hereafter is better and more lasting, giving a specific lasting destination against the nearer life preferred in 87:16.

The section’s named root ص ر ط presents a route with a direction; this verse says to follow the straight path and not other paths that split people from God’s way, making divergence itself the danger.
This verse describes rivers and roads through the land as means of guidance; it gives a concrete landscape version of the section’s path that carries travelers toward an intended direction.
The signs and stars here guide travelers; this specifies how a route can still lead somewhere when the traveler relies on markers rather than direct sight of the destination.
Stars are made for people to find their way through the darknesses of land and sea, a direct navigation scene where the path is not fully visible but has a destination.
The verse says God made roads through the earth so people can travel; this is a physical counterpart to the section’s road as a directed passage.
This verse says God made roads in the earth so people may be guided; it links the road itself with the arrival of guidance, as the section’s straight-path image does.
The verse describes traveling through broad roads in the earth, concretely staging the movement along a way that the section uses to distinguish directed travel from aimless loss.
This verse says God showed the human two high paths; its image of distinct routes sharpens the section’s contrast between going along a path and losing one’s direction.
This verse says the person did not climb the steep pass; 90:12 begins to identify that pass, so this row contributes the refusal to take a difficult route with a moral destination.
The section’s dictionary wording describes someone who went away with no one knowing where; this verse asks فَأَيْنَ تَذْهَبُونَ, directly making the destination of a departure the question.
After the question about where people are going in 81:26, this verse says the reminder is for whoever wills to be upright; it contributes the alternative of choosing a directed course.
The section’s root ض ل ل describes loss of direction; this verse says Satan turned the people away from the way while they thought themselves guided, a specific case of hidden misdirection.
This verse says the Messenger cannot guide blind people out of their error; it parallels the section’s blind people rushing toward a path they cannot see.

This repeats the blind person’s inability to be guided out of error, but adds that only those who believe the signs can be made to hear; it develops the section’s contrast between sightless movement and guidance.
This verse describes deaf and mute people in darkness, then contrasts those God leaves astray with those He places on a straight path; the lost and guided courses are explicit.
People with hearts, eyes, and ears who do not perceive are called more astray than cattle; this gives a specific image of having faculties yet failing to find the way.
Thamud are shown the way but prefer blindness to guidance; this is a specific reversal of the section’s traveler who can pass from sight yet remain on a directed course.
This verse says people found their fathers astray; it makes the section’s lost direction a condition inherited from those who went before.
The next verse says they hasten along their fathers’ footsteps; its contribution is movement along a route inherited from those described as lost in 37:69.
David is told not to follow desire lest it lead him astray from God’s way; the verse specifies how a person can leave a route with a known destination.
This verse describes speech purchased to lead people astray from God’s way; it gives a concrete means by which a traveler can be diverted from the section’s guided road.
Those God leaves astray have no protector, and when they see punishment they ask whether there is a way back; this directly depicts losing both direction and a return route.
The verse says no leaf falls without God knowing it and mentions a grain in earth’s darknesses kept in a clear record; it reverses the section’s image of something hidden as something lost.
This verse describes people created from dust and a dead earth revived into growth; it makes burial and the earth’s apparent lifelessness a passage toward renewed life.
The verse says the Hour is coming and God will raise those in the graves; it directly gives a destination beyond the section’s image of the dead disappearing into earth.
A traveler sees a ruined town and asks how God will give it life after death; God makes him die for a hundred years and revives him, turning apparent disappearance into a demonstrated return.
This verse says God brings the living from the dead and the dead from the living, and revives earth after its death; disappearance is one stage in a repeated passage.
The verse directs attention to traces of mercy and asks how God gives life to earth after its death; it reverses the image of earth as the final place where life disappears.
Winds drive clouds to dead land, and God gives life to the earth after its death; the scene makes lifeless ground a passage to renewed life, paralleling the burial image.
The deniers ask whether they will be created anew after being torn apart; this repeats the section’s question about whether bodily disappearance into fragments is final.
The deniers say only worldly life exists and that time destroys them; this states explicitly the view that disappearance in death has no destination.
The next verse says their only argument when revelation is recited is to demand their forefathers be brought back; it continues their denial that the dead have a destination.
Disbelievers claim they will not be raised, and the answer affirms that they will be raised and informed of what they did; this directly opposes disappearance as an end.
This verse introduces the judgment question of where the claimed partners are; 40:74 gives the answer that they have departed, so this row contributes the search for what has vanished.
At judgment people ask where their claimed partners are and are told those partners have left them; it is another direct scene of an object disappearing from those who relied on it.

This verse stages the gathering of worshippers with the partners they claimed; 10:29 gives the partners’ testimony and 10:30 says the fabrications vanish, so this row contributes the gathering itself.
The claimed partners testify that the worshippers were not worshipping them; this supplies the denial within the gathering scene before 10:30 states that the fabrications vanished.
The verse asks who is further astray than those who call on beings that cannot answer until Resurrection and are unaware of the calls; it depicts reliance on an absent destination.
When people are gathered, the invoked beings become enemies and deny the worship; this completes the nonresponse in 46:5 and the section’s image of vanished claims.
The people who made idols objects of affection in this life disavow and curse one another at Resurrection; it shows the claimed bond disappearing at the final meeting.
The command to remember God when one forgets gives a direct memory-loss instance, matching the section’s dictionary sense of an event disappearing from recollection.
The cupbearer forgets to mention Joseph to the king; this is a concrete event lost from memory, one of the section’s stated secondary senses of ض ل ل.
The verse says those who forget God are made to forget themselves; it develops the section’s connection between what disappears from memory and losing oneself.
When Hell is brought near, a person remembers what he sent ahead; this reverses the section’s forgotten-event image by showing lost memory return at judgment.
God takes souls at death and sleep, retaining those whose death He decrees and returning the others until an appointed term; unseen absence is shown as custody with a defined endpoint.

This verse describes pure milk emerging from between waste and blood; unlike the section’s dictionary example of milk disappearing into water, the milk keeps a distinct identity through a hidden passage.
The promised rivers include milk whose taste does not change; this contrasts the section’s dictionary image of milk losing its identity in water with milk that remains distinct.

The verse uses the image of the calf being made to enter the hearts of the Israelites; as a metaphor, it parallels the section’s swallowed thing disappearing from sight while reaching an inward destination.
